title: Today Rome denies persuasion of own remitted sins as faith-act; Cologne/Cassander dissent noted
source_text: XXXIII. Praeterea Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, hodie saltem, communi consensu ad fidem salvificam & justificantem pertinere nolunt, ut quis persuasus sit se misericordiam a Deo consecutum esse, & sibi remissa esse per Christi gratiam peccata. Ac ejusmodi persuasionem negant esse fidei actum, & potius ad temerariam quandam praesumptionem spectare existimant: nedum ut putent per illam hominem justificari. Fuere tamen nonnulli superiori saeculo in Ecclesia Romana Theologi, iique non incelebres, qui senserunt & scriptis publice mandaverunt ad justificationem hominis omnino requiri, ut homo certo credat, non tantum generaliter quod propter Christum vere poenitentibus remittantur peccata, sed etiam quod ipsi homini remissa sint propter Christum per fidem. Hanc sententiam Georgius Cassander, in consultatione ad articulum quartum Confessionis Augustanae, tribuit Theologis Coloniensibus, quorum verba recitat ex libro quem ediderunt anno superioris saeculi trigesimo sexto in Concilio quodam suae dioeceseos, cuique titulum fecerunt Enchiridion Christianae Religionis. Ubi, teste eodem Cassandro, sic legitur: Dicimus hominem per fidem donum justificationis tum demum accipere, quum & perterrefactus & concussus in poenitentia rursus erigitur per fidem, credens sibi esse remissa peccata propter meritum Christi, qui in se credentibus remissionem peccatorum pollicitus est, & quum novum in se sentit affectum, quo detestatur malum, & carnis infirmitati resistens, ad bonum secundum Deum accenditur, tametsi affectus nondum perfectus sit.
pass_a_gloss: Moreover the doctors of the Roman Church, at least today, by common consent refuse to hold that it belongs to saving and justifying faith that someone be persuaded he has obtained mercy from God and that his sins have been remitted to him through the grace of Christ. And they deny that such persuasion is an act of faith, and think it rather looks toward a certain rash presumption; still less do they think a person is justified through it. Yet there were some theologians in the Roman Church in the previous century, and not obscure ones, who thought and publicly committed to writing that for a person justification it is altogether required that the person firmly believe not only in general that sins are remitted to the truly penitent on account of Christ, but also that sins have been remitted to that very person on account of Christ through faith. George Cassander, in his consultation on the fourth article of the Augsburg Confession, attributes this view to the Cologne theologians, whose words he recites from a book they published in the thirty-sixth year of the previous century in a council of their diocese, titled Enchiridion Christianae Religionis. There, according to Cassander, it reads: We say that a person receives the gift of justification through faith only when, terrified and shaken in repentance, he is raised again by faith, believing that his sins are remitted on account of Christ merit, who promised remission of sins to those who believe in him, and when he feels in himself a new affection by which he detests evil and, resisting the weakness of the flesh, is kindled toward the good according to God, even if the affection is not yet perfect.
pass_b_english: Present Roman consensus refuses to make persuasion that one has obtained mercy and remitted sins part of saving justifying faith; such persuasion is treated as rash presumption, not the act by which one is justified.

Cassander cites earlier Cologne Enchiridion theologians who required believing not only general remission for penitents in Christ, but also that one own sins are remitted through faith, together with a new penitent affection.

lemmas.gloss: they deny that such persuasion is an act of faith

choices.why: Modern Rome vs older Cologne requirement.
rejected: certainty of own remitted sins as essential faith-act
